def: A law passed by Parliament. Each Act is divided into numbered sections.
eg: The Penal Code is an Act.

def: Kenya's main criminal law. It defines offences such as murder, theft and criminal defamation, and sets their punishments.
eg: Section 204 sets the punishment for murder.

def: The 2006 Act that defines sexual offences and their sentences, many of them minimum sentences.
eg: Section 8 is defilement (sexual offences against children).

def: The Kenya Information and Communications Act, which regulates telecoms and broadcasting.
eg: Section 29 (improper use of a telecom system) was struck down in Andare, 2016.

def: The supreme law. Any Act that conflicts with it can be declared invalid by a court. Its parts are called Articles, not sections.
A numbered paragraph of an Act, and a numbered part inside it. Courts often rule on just one subsection.
The number an Act has in the Laws of Kenya collection. We use it in our IDs.
eg: Cap. 63 is the Penal Code, so its ID is ke/act/cap-63.

def: The current wording of an Act with all amendments folded in. Kenya Law publishes it, but it doesn't record court rulings. That gap is why this project exists.
Parliament changing a section's words (amendment) or removing it altogether (repeal). Kenya Law does record these, in editorial notes.
A lawyer's phrase for a law or case you can still rely on: it hasn't been struck down, overruled or repealed.
A court finds that a section conflicts with the Constitution, and so it has no force. It can be the whole section or only part of it.
The standard wording of a partial declaration. Only the part the court describes is invalid; the rest of the section still stands.
eg: Okuta: s.194 is invalid "to the extent that it covers offences other than…"

def: Instead of striking words out, the court gives them a narrower meaning so that they fit the Constitution. The section survives, but not as its plain words suggest.
eg: Kilwake: the minimum sentences in SOA s.8 "must be interpreted so as not to take away the discretion of the court".

def: The court cuts specific words out of a section and keeps the rest.
Someone challenged the section and the court found it constitutional. It is still in force, and now it has been tested.
The part of a judgment that actually decides the case: the declarations and orders, usually at the end. It's the part we quote.
A sentence the law says a judge must give, with no choice. Muruatetu held the mandatory death sentence for murder unconstitutional.
The lowest sentence a law allows. The Sexual Offences Act sets many, which is what the s.8 cases were about.
Telling someone what they should do about their own legal situation. LexHack never does this. It reports what published sources say.
The court that hears most constitutional petitions in the first instance. It can declare an Act unconstitutional.
Hears appeals from the High Court. Its rulings bind the High Court.
Kenya's highest court. Its rulings bind every other court.
A court's written decision, with its reasons and its orders.
How a case asking the court to declare a law unconstitutional usually starts.
A higher court, hearing an appeal in the same case, sets the lower court's decision aside. The earlier ruling stops counting.
eg: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal in Mwangi (2024).

def: Lower courts must follow higher courts' rulings. So a Supreme Court ruling in one case can cancel a Court of Appeal reading from another case, with no appeal between them.
Latin for "through lack of care". A court's finding that an earlier decision overlooked binding law, so it need not be followed.
Further instructions a court gives later in the same case, often to explain how far its ruling reaches.
eg: The 2021 Muruatetu directions limit the 2017 ruling to murder.

def: A standard reference for a judgment: year, court and number.
Kenya Law's older citation format. It gives the year but not the court or number, so matching one to a judgment means using the party names.
eg: Francis Karioko Muruatetu & another v Republic [2017] eKLR

def: A court applying a higher court's decision without deciding anything new itself. It's the classifier's most common mistake: it isn't an event on the section.
eg: A sentencing appeal that applies Muruatetu.

def: A tool that tells you whether a law or case is still good law, and which later decisions affected it. The US has Shepard's and KeyCite. Kenya has none; LexHack is one.
The official publisher of Kenya's laws and judgments (new.kenyalaw.org). Its statute pages are our source text.
A document given to a court: submissions, pleadings, a petition. The filing checker reads these.
Reads a legal document and runs three checks on each citation: does the case exist, is the quote really in it, and is the section still good law.
A case or quote that an AI tool made up. It looks real but doesn't exist. Courts in several countries have sanctioned lawyers for filing them.
One place a judgment cites a section. A mention says nothing about what the court did to the section.
eg: A murder trial mentions s.204 in almost every judgment.

def: Something a court (or Parliament) actually did to a section: declared it unconstitutional, read it down, upheld it, reversed an earlier ruling. Events are the heart of the project.
Where a section stands today. It's never stored: it's worked out from the section's events each time, using Kenya's rules.
A small, hand-checked set of correct answers. We use it to score the automatic pipeline and as reliable demo data.
A judgment that mentions a section but does nothing to it. It catches the easiest mistake: treating a mention as an event.
Verified rows were checked by a person against the judgment. Extracted rows were found by the pipeline. The API leaves extracted rows out unless asked, and then labels them unverified.
Test data kept aside and never used to tune the code, so the score on it is honest.
The country whose law it is. Every ID starts with it (ke), so the design can extend beyond Kenya.
An event the pipeline found that no person has checked yet. It's shown with a warning, never used as a section's status by default.
eg: 120 leads so far, about 80% of them right.

def: A second LLM call that re-reads each extracted event and asks only: is this the court's own holding, and on the section claimed? Events it fails are hidden. It lifted precision from 59% to about 80%.
Two people judge the same sample without seeing each other's answers or the machine's reasoning. Where they agree, that's the answer; where they don't, it's counted as unclear.
The next piece of the website: a list of unverified leads where a person confirms or rejects each one, turning good leads into verified events.
A non-profit that saves copies of web pages. All our bulk data came from its copies of Kenya Law, not from Kenya Law directly.
The standard file format for storing fetched web pages byte for byte. We keep the raw pages so we can re-parse without fetching again.
An international format for legal documents. Kenya Law uses it, which is why every section has a machine-readable ID.
The ID of a section in Kenya Law's pages. It stays the same across versions, which lets us follow one section through time.
The text of an Act on one date. The Penal Code has three versions we hold: 2014, 2022 and 2023.
Our ID for one section: jurisdiction, Act and eId joined together.
A plain spreadsheet file: one row per line, columns separated by commas. Our answer keys are CSVs so people can read and edit them.
A plain-text format for structured data. The API answers in JSON, and this site's demo data is JSON.
Postgres is the database. Neon is the company hosting it for us.
A text pattern. We use them to find citations like "section 204 of the Penal Code" in judgment text.

A large language model. We use one for what patterns can't do: working out which law a bare "section 39" means, and what a court did to a section (DeepSeek, with a second pass that checks each answer). Every quote it returns is checked word for word.
A list of numbers that captures what a text means, so similar meanings sit close together. It lets search find "sentence for killing a person" → s.204.
Searching by exact words and by meaning at once, then merging the two lists (reciprocal rank fusion).
Of everything the extractor found, the share that was right.
Of everything that was really there, the share the extractor found.
The door the website uses to ask the database questions. Ours is built with FastAPI; this site uses a copy of its answers.
Saved answers from the LLM and embedding services, so re-running costs nothing. It lives in $LEXHACK_DATA, which the team shares through Cloudflare R2, not git.
Online file storage the team uses to share $LEXHACK_DATA (raw pages, parsed files, caches). scripts/sync.sh pulls and pushes; pull before working, push after.
